messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Version 2.2-3 of ergm on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  A new version of ergm (version 2.2-3) just went up on CRAN.   
This version has a few new features that might be of interest:

(1) There are new simulate.formula and simulate.ergm functions that  
allow a bit more control over output of simulated networks and that  
should increase efficiency if only network statistics are desired.   
Mostly, this change will be invisible, but if you simulate random  
network statistics using statsonly=TRUE then you may notice an  
improvement in speed.

(2) In response to a couple of requests from this list, there is now a  
function, called ergmMPLE, that will return the response and  
predictors (the latter is sometimes called the matrix of change  
statistics) that can be plugged into a logistic regression routine to  
obtain the MPLE (maximum pseudolikelihood estimate).  Check ?ergmMPLE  
for details.

(3) There is a new algorithm for fitting ERGMs, called "stepping",  
that is implemented as a 'style' in the control.ergm function.  See ? 
control.ergm for details.  This algorithm is described in a tech  
report:  http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/step.pdf

(4) Assorted odds and ends, used for various and sundry purposes:   
Check out ?is.inCH, ?wtd.median, ?ecoli


Already, there are a few bugs that I did not fix before uploading the  
new version.  Thus, another new version (2.2-4) will go up in just a  
few days.  So I'm curious:  Are there bugs that we've missed, or  
simple additions that would be helpful?  If so, I might be able to  
fix / add them before the next release.

Thanks in advance,
Dave

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] are ergm's parameters and change statistics standardized?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Guido,

I was looking at this very same problem this past week. There are a number
of different methods for standardizing log-odds coefficients. Most of these
require information about the standard deviation of the independent
variable, the dependent variable, or both. The problem with ergm models is
that we do not know the standard deviation of the network-structural
independent variables of the model.

Menard (2004) has proposed an information-based method for standardizing
log-odds coefficients. The advantage of using this method with ergm
coefficients is that it does not require an estimate of the standard
deviation of the independent variable, just the log-likelihood values from
the set of all possible nested models. The disadvantage is that with even
modest numbers of covariates the number of models that must be run can
become cumbersome.

Perhaps someone more versed in ergm statistics will respond on the
appropriateness of this method for ergm coefficients.

A further question I have on this subject is, What is the appropriate Null
model to use for these types of comparisons? The null deviance in the ergm
output appears to be based on an Erdos-Renyi random graph with p = 0.5.
However, the literature I've been reading on standardizing logistic
regression coefficients appears ambiguous on what is meant by the "null"
model. In some cases, it appears to mean the model with the theoretical
maximum deviance; in other cases the null model is described as a model
fitted "without parameters", but apparently including an intercept term
(i.e. edges, in the ergm case). (For an example of this ambiguity, see
Nagelkerke's (1991) generalized R-squared.)

Cheers,
Dave

Menard, Scott. 2004. Six approaches to calculating standardized logistic
regression coefficients. The American Statistician, 58: 218-223.

Nagelkerke, N.J.D. 1991. A note on a general definition of the coefficient
of determination. Biometrika, 78: 691-692.

____________________________
David A. Nolin
Postdoctoral Scholar
Carolina Population Center
University of North Carolina

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dave -

dnolin wrote:
> A further question I have on this subject is, What is the appropriate Null
> model to use for these types of comparisons? The null deviance in the ergm
> output appears to be based on an Erdos-Renyi random graph with p = 0.5.
> However, the literature I've been reading on standardizing logistic
> regression coefficients appears ambiguous on what is meant by the "null"
> model. In some cases, it appears to mean the model with the theoretical
> maximum deviance; in other cases the null model is described as a model
> fitted "without parameters", but apparently including an intercept term
> (i.e. edges, in the ergm case). (For an example of this ambiguity, see
> Nagelkerke's (1991) generalized R-squared.)

As is always the case, your null should be based on the baseline process 
against which you wish to test.  The null on which the ergm() parameter 
p-values are based is a model in which all parameters but the indicated 
one are fixed at their MLEs, with the indicated parameter being fixed at 
0 (i.e., the associated statistic is not in the model).  As far as the 
null _deviance_, this is indeed based on the uniform random graph 
(conditional on number of vertices).  Nothing prevents one, however, 
from comparing one's fitted model to other baselines, such as the 
maximum likelihood homogeneous Bernoulli graph (i.e., the model with 
only an edge term), a degree distribution model, etc.  Indeed, Holland 
and Leinhardt's original paper suggests the use of the p1 family as a 
null model against which to test a hypothesis of excess triangulation 
(something that could not be estimated directly at the time, although 
they discuss the possibility).  Note that they suggest performing this 
test in the mean value space, not the natural parameter space, since (as 
noted) they could not fit models with dyadic dependence.

Testing in the mean value space is also the logic behind conditional 
uniform graph tests, and the use of general ERGMs as nulls in this 
manner is a natural extension to this philosophy (and, indeed, can be 
thought of generalized baseline models in a "pure" Mayhewan sense, since 
they maximize entropy given the support and mean stats).  The model 
adequacy checks in ergm.gof() can be viewed in this light.  Choosing an 
appropriate baseline model is as much a matter of substantive theory as 
statistics per se, and your choice should reflect your knowledge of the 
system under study (e.g., through the "obvious" baseline effects that 
are known to be present, and which must be discounted before concluding 
that something more interesting is afoot).  For this reason, there can 
be no universally "correct" null.

In general, my sense is that one is better served by reasoning about 
these models from first principles, than by trying to directly import 
ideas from the logistic regression world sans attention to context. 
That's not to say that no such concepts can be brought over -- after 
all, the logistic case is a special case of the discrete exponential 
family framework -- but techniques developed for a world of independent, 
non-relational variables can often be misleading and/or useless when 
dealing with network data.  Start with what you know and what you want 
to measure.  If this leads you back to a problem for which a known (and 
applicable) solution exists in the logistic/GLM literature, great!  If 
not, then trying to apply an inapplicable technique from conventional 
regression is probably going to get you in trouble.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Feng Luo wrote:
> Dear All:

> Sorry to bother you again!
> 
> I learned a ERGM model from a fully connected network. Is there a way I 
> can guarantee my simulated networks are also fully connected?

Yes: simulate normally, and subsequently filter out only the connected 
graphs (using is.connected or the like to identify those you need to 
keep).  This is a trivial rejection sampling scheme, and will give you 
draws from the model conditional on being connected.

(Note, however, that this is not the same as _fitting_ a model 
conditional on the graph being fully connected (i.e., a model whose 
support is on the connected graphs of order matching the observed 
graph).  For that, you would need to use an MCMC proposal that preserved 
connectedness.  I don't believe we have one of those at present, 
although I could be mistaken.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi Victorin.  In your attachment, situations 2 through 5 give  
different answers for esp(2) and dsp(2).  The direction of the arc  
from node A to node B is important.

Situation 2:  A 2-esp is counted only if the two 2-paths from A to B  
go in the same direction as this arc, as in this situation.
Situation 3:  If both of the 2-paths go in the opposite direction as  
the arc from A to B, then this counts as a 2-dsp (because B->A is a  
dyad without an edge) but not a 2-esp.
Situations 4 and 5: Finally, if the only two 2-paths from A to B go in  
opposite directions, then there is no 2-esp nor 2-dsp.

Here is some code that verifies this:

 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 2
 > m[1,3]=m[3,2]=m[1,4]=m[4,2]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    1    1
 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 3
 > m[2,3]=m[3,1]=m[2,4]=m[4,1]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    0    1
 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 4
 > m[1,3]=m[3,2]=m[2,4]=m[4,1]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    0    0
 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 5
 > m[2,3]=m[3,1]=m[1,4]=m[4,2]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    0    0


Hope this helps.
Dave

Hi Annie.  Not silly at all -- in fact, this is a vexing problem that  
we've seen before.

Here's what's happening:  When you read in TestVec, it is created as  
an object of type "data.frame".  Then, when you try to coerce it to  
type "vector", essentially nothing happens.  (In particular, the thing  
you think has happened, has not.)  You can verify this by typing  
class(TestVec), when you'll see that it is STILL a data.frame.  This  
is something of an R quirk.  I'm sure there is a reason for it, but  
I'm not sure what the reason is.

In any case, If you replace your line
TestVec = as.vector(TestVec)

by, say,
TestVec = as.vector(TestVec[,1]) # Convert just the first column in  
the data frame

or alternatively
TestVec = as.vector(as.matrix(TestVec)) # Convert data.frame to matrix  
to vector

then your example should work.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Feng,

I just tried fitting your formula, with some well-tuned fitting 
parameters, and I was able to get good model estimates in a couple of 
hours.  This was on a unix cluster, though.  The exact call I used was:

formula <- fmh ~ edges + nodefactor("Grade") + nodefactor("Race") + 
nodefactor("Sex")  + nodematch("Grade",diff=T)  + nodematch("Sex",diff=F) 
+ gwdegree(1.0,fixed=T) + gwesp(1.0,fixed=T) + gwdsp(1.0,fixed=T)

fit <- ergm(formula, burnin = 10000, interval = 1000, MCMCsamplesize = 
2500, maxit = 25, control = control.ergm(steplength = .25))

and the diagnostics are attached, so you can see it worked well.

There's a bit of a learning curve behind knowing what ergm fitting 
parameters to tweak to get model convergence as quickly as possible. I 
like taking the general approach I use here with the gw* terms, though; a 
larger sample size, a high maxit, and a smaller steplength; it seems to 
work for me in general.

Try this specific run and see how long it takes for you.  If it doesn't 
converge or takes a really really long time, then you may want to try to 
get access to a more powerful machine somehow.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Goodness of fit with directed networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Balasz.  Good question.  gof does work with directed networks, but  
I see that the documentation is not good for explaining how this  
works.  I ought to fix this in a future version of ergm.

By typing
gof_model_rok1 <- gof(model_rok1)
you are using the default value of the "GOF" argument, which means  
you're essentially typing

gof_model_rok1 <- gof(model_rok1, GOF = ~degree + espartners + distance)

and, as you saw, this generates an error because "degree" is an  
undirected-network statistic.  What you can do is replace "degree" by  
"odegree" and/or "idegree" (outdegree or indegree), or neither, by  
typing, say,

gof_model_rok1 <- gof(model_rok1, GOF = ~idegree + odegree +  
espartners + distance)

Other options are "dspartners" for dyadic shared partners and  
"triadcensus" for a census of the sixteen types of triads possible in  
a directed network.  The explanation of the triads is found under  
"triadcensus" in ?ergm-terms.

Sorry the gof documentation is lacking!

Dave
